# Session 8: Hands-on: LLM Classification & Prompt Iteration

## 📋 Agenda

- Run LLM-based text classification in Colab
- Evaluate the outputs with the prepared tools
- Get your Gemini API key

## 🎯 Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

- Get and store a **Gemini API key** (Colab Secrets) and make **reproducible** calls (`temperature=0`, `seed`).
- Run the **zero-shot → few-shot → chain-of-thought** progression on CEFR, re-evaluating each on a validation set.
- Score the final prompt **once** on the held-out test set.
- Prompt for **structured output** and recognise **JSON** as the `{id, text, label}` format.

# From feedback to classification

## The same components, a new task {.smaller}

The CEFR prompt you'll write is **Huang & Mizumoto's Ex 2 structure**, re-cast for classification:

| Ex 2 — writing feedback (S7) | CEFR classification (today) |
|---|---|
| **Directive:** "review and give feedback" | "classify this sentence's **CEFR level**" |
| **Additional information:** the 5-item Criteria rubric | the **CEFR level descriptors** |
| **Input data:** "My paragraph" | the learner **sentence** `{text}` |
| **Output formatting:** "only feedback, no rewrite" | "**return only the label**" → structured / JSON |

. . .

And the **few-shot examples** are **written by you**, never taken from the set you score on (contamination, S7).

# Your Gemini API key

## Today you call the model yourself

Days 1–2 needed no key: Day 1 used Colab's built-in model, Day 2 used a **frozen** prediction file.

. . .

From today you make the calls yourself, so they must be **reproducible**. We move to the Gemini API, where `temperature` and `seed` can be set.

## Four steps, five minutes

1. Go to **Google AI Studio** → *Get API key* → create one.
2. In Colab: the **🔑 key icon** in the left sidebar (Secrets).
3. Name it exactly `GEMINI_API_KEY`, paste the value.
4. Toggle **Notebook access** on.

. . .

Re-run the Setup cell. It should say `LLM backend: api`.

::: {.callout-note}
Full walkthrough with screenshots: [`resources/tools/gemini-api-key.md`](../resources/tools/gemini-api-key.md)
:::

## Why a key at all {.smaller}

|  | Colab's built-in model | Gemini API (today) |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | none | a key, once |
| `temperature` | not exposed | **`0`** |
| `seed` | not exposed | **`42`** |
| Same prompt twice | may differ | same answer |

. . .

Reproducibility is a requirement here: **someone else must be able to re-run your work and get your reported numbers.**

## Two separate rate limits {.smaller}

The free tier limits you **two independent ways**:

- **RPM** — 15 requests per *minute*
- **RPD** — 500 requests per *day*

. . .

Most unexpected `429` errors come from the **per-minute** limit, while the daily limit is still far from reached.

. . .

`generate_text` has been spacing out your calls and retrying since Day 1. You will read the code that does this in the notebook.

# Run classification in Colab

## Two sets, two purposes {.smaller}

| File | Size | What it is for |
|---|:--:|---|
| `val` | 24 | **Tune on this.** Every prompt you try is scored here. |
| `gold` | 72 | **Report on this.** Used once, at the very end. |

. . .

If you try five prompts on the 72 and keep the best, that score is no longer an estimate of performance on *new* sentences, because you selected the prompt using those 72 items.

. . .

Tune on the validation set, and report once on the test set. This is the split from S7, now as two files.

## Round 0 — zero-shot

Just describe the task.

``` python
PROMPT_ZERO = """You are an expert rater of English sentence
difficulty using the CEFR scale.
Classify the sentence into exactly one of: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2.
Answer with the level only.

Sentence: {text}"""

pred_zero = run_prompt(PROMPT_ZERO, val)
evaluate(val, pred_zero, ordered=True)
```

. . .

`{text}` marks the position where each sentence is inserted. **Keep it in your prompt.**

## Round 1 — few-shot

Add labelled examples so the model can infer the pattern.

``` python
Examples:
Sentence: "I have a cat." -> A1
Sentence: "She went to the shops because she needed milk." -> A2
Sentence: "The results suggest a modest improvement." -> B2
```

. . .

Write your own. Do **not** copy one from `val` or `gold`: that gives the model the answers to the items you will test it on.

## Round 2 — chain-of-thought

Ask it to reason first, then answer.

``` python
Think step by step about the vocabulary and grammar,
then decide the level.
Do NOT mention any other CEFR level while reasoning.
End with the final level on its own.
```

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
`run_prompt` keeps the **first** CEFR level it sees in the reply. That is why the prompt forbids mentioning others — otherwise the *parser*, not the model, produces the error.
:::

# Evaluate the outputs

## Read the report, not just the average {.smaller}

`evaluate` prints per-class precision, recall and F1 — then macro-F1, plain κ and weighted κ.

. . .

**Macro-F1 averages the classes equally.** One level with F1 near zero lowers the whole number, and the per-class report shows you *which* level it is.

. . .

Fill in the table as you go:

| Iteration | macro-F1 (val) |
|---|:--:|
| 0 · zero-shot | … |
| 1 · few-shot | … |
| 2 · chain-of-thought | … |

## The held-out run — once

Pick your best prompt. Score it on the 72.

``` python
pred_test = run_prompt(BEST_PROMPT, gold)
evaluate(gold, pred_test, ordered=True)
```

. . .

Expect it to be **lower** than your validation score.

. . .

That difference is not a mistake. It is the expected effect of having chosen a prompt by looking at validation results. If you read this number and then edit the prompt again, the 72 items are no longer held out.

## Structured output

So far the model returns a bare label. For real pipelines you want it to return **data**:

``` json
{"id": 17, "label": "B2"}
```

. . .

That is the same `{id, text, label}` schema from Day 1 — **JSON** is just the file format it travels in.

. . .

Asking for JSON is *output formatting* (one of S7's prompt components). It makes the reply readable by code, instead of text you have to interpret.
